claim: Wrapping of DNA into nucleosomes restricts accessibility to DNA and may affect the recognition of binding motifs by transcription factors.
source: Wrapping of DNA into nucleosomes restricts accessibility to DNA and may affect the recognition of binding motifs by transcription factors.
evidence: This is a well-established principle in chromatin biology, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: Pioneer transcription factors can specifically recognize their DNA binding sites on nucleosomes.
source: A certain class of transcription factors, the pioneer transcription factors, can specifically recognize their DNA binding sites on nucleosomes, initiate local chromatin opening, and facilitate the binding of co-factors in a cell-type-specific manner.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pioneer transcription factors initiate local chromatin opening.
source: A certain class of transcription factors, the pioneer transcription factors, can specifically recognize their DNA binding sites on nucleosomes, initiate local chromatin opening, and facilitate the binding of co-factors in a cell-type-specific manner.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: Pioneer transcription factors facilitate the binding of co-factors in a cell-type-specific manner.
source: A certain class of transcription factors, the pioneer transcription factors, can specifically recognize their DNA binding sites on nucleosomes, initiate local chromatin opening, and facilitate the binding of co-factors in a cell-type-specific manner.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the field.

claim: For the majority of human pioneer transcription factors, the locations of their binding sites, mechanisms of binding, and regulation remain unknown.
source: For the majority of human pioneer transcription factors, the locations of their binding sites, mechanisms of binding, and regulation remain unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, supported by inference from the literature.

claim: A computational method was developed to predict the cell-type-specific ability of transcription factors to bind nucleosomes by integrating ChIP-seq, MNase-seq, and DNase-seq data with details of nucleosome structure.
source: We have developed a computational method to predict the cell-type-specific ability of transcription factors to bind nucleosomes by integrating ChIP-seq, MNase-seq, and DNase-seq data with details of nucleosome structure.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data and methods described in the manuscript.

claim: The computational approach can discriminate pioneer from canonical transcription factors.
source: We have demonstrated the ability of our approach in discriminating pioneer from canonical transcription factors and predicted new potential pioneer transcription factors in H1, K562, HepG2, and HeLa-S3 cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by the validation results presented in the manuscript using known PTFs as benchmarks.

claim: New potential pioneer transcription factors were predicted in H1, K562, HepG2, and HeLa-S3 cell lines.
source: We have demonstrated the ability of our approach in discriminating pioneer from canonical transcription factors and predicted new potential pioneer transcription factors in H1, K562, HepG2, and HeLa-S3 cell lines.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the computational analysis and data.

claim: Six clusters of distinctive binding sites on nucleosomal DNA were detected for various pioneer transcription factors.
source: Last, we systematically analyzed the interaction modes between various pioneer transcription factors and detected several clusters of distinctive binding sites on nucleosomal DNA.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nucleosomes comprise a histone octamer of four types of core histones of two copies each, and ~147 bp of DNA wrapped around them.
source: They comprise a histone octamer of four types of core histones of two copies each, and ~147 bp of DNA wrapped around them (Luger et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation to Luger et al., 1997.

claim: Intrinsically disordered histone tails may modulate DNA accessibility by forming transient interactions with the nucleosomal and linker DNA.
source: Intrinsically disordered histone tails flank histone core domains and may also modulate DNA accessibility by forming transient interactions with the nucleosomal and linker DNA (Peng et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peng et al., 2021a.

claim: Rapid transcription activation may occur by relatively small changes of DNA solvent exposure.
source: Indeed, rapid transcription activation may occur by relatively small changes of DNA solvent exposure, and localized nucleosomal array structures can be dynamically exposed without the large-scale chromatin rearrangements (Zaret, 2020; Iwafuchi-Doi, 2019; Kono and Ishida, 2020; Chereji et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Localized nucleosomal array structures can be dynamically exposed without large-scale chromatin rearrangements.
source: Indeed, rapid transcription activation may occur by relatively small changes of DNA solvent exposure, and localized nucleosomal array structures can be dynamically exposed without the large-scale chromatin rearrangements (Zaret, 2020; Iwafuchi-Doi, 2019; Kono and Ishida, 2020; Chereji et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Pioneer transcription factors play critical roles in mediating cell-type-specific gene expression and establishment of cell lineage reprogramming.
source: Several studies have revealed the critical roles of PTFs in mediating the cell-type-specific gene expression and establishment of cell lineage reprogramming (Peñalosa-Ruiz et al., 2019; Balsalobre and Drouin, 2022; Jaenisch and Young, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The vast majority of TFs preferably bind naked DNA instead of nucleosomal DNA at physiological concentrations.
source: It has been revealed that the vast majority of TFs preferably bind naked DNA instead of nucleosomal DNA at physiological concentrations, whereas certain TFs specifically target nucleosomes at different locations and orientations (Zhu et al., 2018; Meers et al., 2019; Soufi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Certain TFs specifically target nucleosomes at different locations and orientations.
source: It has been revealed that the vast majority of TFs preferably bind naked DNA instead of nucleosomal DNA at physiological concentrations, whereas certain TFs specifically target nucleosomes at different locations and orientations (Zhu et al., 2018; Meers et al., 2019; Soufi et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Several structures of PTFs in complex with nucleosomes have recently been resolved.
source: Moreover, several structures of PTFs in complex with nucleosomes have recently been resolved (Min and Liu, 2021; Michael et al., 2020; Dodonova et al., 2020; Tanaka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple structural studies.

claim: The interaction modes of most TFs with nucleosomes remain obscure.
source: Despite significant advances in recent experimental approaches, the interaction modes of most TFs with nucleosomes remain obscure and their cell-type-specific pioneer activities are largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Cell-type-specific pioneer activities of most TFs are largely unknown.
source: Despite significant advances in recent experimental approaches, the interaction modes of most TFs with nucleosomes remain obscure and their cell-type-specific pioneer activities are largely unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: DNA binding sites of PTFs should not be depleted and, in some cases, should be enriched on nucleosome regions.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that DNA binding sites of PTFs should not be depleted and, in some cases, should be enriched on nucleosome regions (NRs).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known properties of PTFs.

claim: Canonical TFs that preferentially bind to naked DNA should exhibit depletion of binding sites on NRs and enrichment in nucleosome-free regions.
source: At the same time, those canonical TFs that can preferentially bind to the naked DNA should exhibit the depletion of binding sites on NRs and enrichment in nucleosome-free regions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the known properties of canonical TFs.

claim: The enrichment score of 32 known PTFs from Test set 1 was significantly higher than for other factors (p-value = 2.12*10–7 for all TFs and p-value = 4.33*10–5 for highly expressed TFs).
source: The enrichment score of the 32 known PTFs from Test set 1 was found to be significantly higher than for other factors (p-value = 2.12*10–7 for all TFs and p-value = 4.33*10–5 for highly expressed TFs, Mann-Whitney U test, Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1—table 7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The enrichment scores show efficiency in classification of PTFs with ROC AUC = 0.69, PR AUC = 0.33 and maximal MCC = 0.31 for all TFs.
source: The results also show the efficiency of enrichment scores for the classification of PTFs (Supplementary file 1—table 7, receiver operating curve [ROC] AUC = 0.69, precision-recall [PR] AUC = 0.33 and maximal Matthews correlation coefficient [MCC] = 0.31 for all TFs and ROC AUC = 0.71, PR AUC = 0.37 and maximal MCC = 0.31 for significantly expressed TFs).
evidence: This is supported by the ROC and PR curve analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The classification accuracy increases from ROC AUC = 0.69 to 0.89 upon the inclusion of differentially open regions compared to open regions.
source: As can be seen in Figure 2 and Supplementary file 1—table 7, it is indeed the case and the classification accuracy increases from ROC AUC = 0.69 to 0.89 (from 0.71 to 0.92 for expressed TFs) upon the inclusion of differentially open regions compared to open regions (maximal MCC increased from 0.31 to 0.42).
evidence: This is supported by the ROC curve analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Known PTFs that acted as key regulators of cell differentiation had the highest enrichment scores.
source: We found that known PTFs that acted as key regulators of cell differentiation had the highest enrichment scores in our ranking (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 2c.

claim: GATA1 and GATA2 showed the highest enrichment scores among PTFs from the FOXA, GATA, and CEBP families.
source: These cases (Test set 2) mainly included PTFs from the FOXA, GATA, and CEBP families (Costa et al., 2003; Smale, 2010; Lee et al., 2005) with GATA1 and GATA2 showing the highest enrichment scores.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis and citations to prior literature.

claim: PTFs in Test set 3 showed significantly lower enrichment scores compared to other TFs.
source: Interestingly, PTFs in Test set 3 (responsible for the maintenance of embryonic stem cell or reprogramming of somatic cells) showed significantly lower enrichment scores compared to other TFs (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Yamanaka PTFs (POU5F1/OCT4 and KLF4) were strongly depleted at nucleosomes.
source: Yamanaka PTFs (POU5F1/OCT4 and KLF4) (Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006) were strongly depleted at nucleosomes (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 2c and citation to Takahashi and Yamanaka, 2006.

claim: Yamanaka PTFs might recognize partial sequence motifs on nucleosomal DNA and require other factors for their binding to nucleosomes.
source: It has been previously shown that Yamanaka PTFs might recognize partial sequence motifs on nucleosomal DNA and require other factors for their binding to nucleosomes (Soufi et al., 2015) and therefore their enrichment score might not be expected to be high.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soufi et al., 2015.

claim: ESSRB and Yamanaka PTF POU5F1 (OCT4) showed significantly higher enrichment scores when differentially open regions were redefined as those closed in differentiated cell lines and open in H1 embryonic cell line.
source: However, when we repeated our analysis by redefining differentially open regions as those closed in differentiated cell lines and open in H1 embryonic cell line, then ESSRB and Yamanaka PTF POU5F1 (OCT4) showed significantly higher enrichment scores (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Using enrichment analysis on differentially active enhancer regions led to worse performance of PTF classification compared to using differentially open chromatin regions.
source: Since PTFs often target enhancers, we have repeated the enrichment analysis using NRs located in differentially active enhancer regions and NDRs located in the conserved active enhancer regions but it led to the worse performance of the PTF classification (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: TFs from cluster 3 (strong binders to naked DNA but weak binders to nucleosomal DNA) had the lowest enrichment scores.
source: We found that TFs from their cluster 3 had the lowest enrichment scores although this trend was not statistically significant because of a lack of the data in this cluster.
evidence: This is supported by comparison with data from Fernandez Garcia et al., 2019.

claim: Half of TFs in clusters 1 and 2 had binding sites enriched on NRs, including known PTFs FOXA1, GATA4, and CEBPA.
source: As to TFs in clusters 1 and 2, half of them had binding sites enriched on NRs (including known PTFs FOXA1, GATA4, and CEBPA) which corresponded to strong nucleosome binders, and another half had binding sites enriched on NDRs (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in Figure 2e.

claim: 39 TFs in H1, K562, HepG2, and HeLa-S3 cell lines ranked highly in enrichment analysis and were significantly expressed in the corresponding cell lines.
source: Using gene expression data from the Roadmap Epigenomics Program (Bernstein et al., 2010) and enrichment analysis on all open chromatin regions, we have identified 39 TFs in H1, K562, HepG2, and HeLa-S3 cell lines (no expression data was available for MCF-7) that ranked highly in the enrichment analysis and were also significantly expressed in the corresponding cell lines (Supplementary file 1—table 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis using gene expression data from the Roadmap Epigenomics Program.

claim: Among 39 identified TFs, 15 TFs were well-characterized PTFs such as GATA, FOXA, and CEBP factors, ESRRB, NEUROD1, SPI1, and subunits of the AP-1 complex.
source: Among these 39 TFs, 15 TFs were well-characterized PTFs such as GATA, FOXA, and CEBP factors, ESRRB, NEUROD1, SPI1, and subunits of the AP-1 complex.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis and established knowledge about these TFs.

claim: RFX5 had the ability to displace nucleosomes.
source: To validate the remaining 20 PTF predictions, we performed literature searches and found that RFX5 had the ability to displace nucleosomes (Zhu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhu et al., 2018.

claim: Many predicted PTFs, such as ZKSCAN1, USF1, USF2, and SRF, were confirmed by a recent study.
source: In addition, many of the predicted PTFs, such as ZKSCAN1, USF1, USF2, and SRF, were confirmed by a recent study (Pop et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pop et al., 2023.

claim: 40 TFs were identified that could act as PTFs with essential roles in cell differentiation in K562, HepG2, and HeLa-S3 cell lines.
source: Next, using the enrichment score calculated based on NRs located in differentially open chromatin regions and NDRs located in conserved open chromatin regions, we identified 40 TFs that could act as PTFs with essential roles in cell differentiation in K562, HepG2, and HeLa-S3 cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Among 40 identified TFs, 15 were well-characterized PTFs including GATA, FOXA, and CEBP factors and subunits of AP-1 complex.
source: Among these 40 TFs, 15 were well-characterized PTFs including GATA, FOXA, and CEBP factors and subunits of AP-1 complex.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis and established knowledge about these TFs.

claim: For the remaining 25 PTF predictions, 7 TFs were annotated in the literature as potential PTFs and/or potential nucleosome binders.
source: For the remaining 25 PTF predictions, 7 TFs were annotated in the literature as potential PTFs and/or potential nucleosome binders (Supplementary file 1—table 8).
evidence: This is supported by literature searches and citations.

claim: HNF4A was annotated as a potential PTF active in chromatin remodeling in the liver.
source: For instance, HNF4A was annotated as a potential PTF active in chromatin remodeling in the liver (Qu et al., 2021), LEF1 was identified as a regulatory high mobility group box protein that could bind to nucleosomes (Steger and Workman, 1997), and CUX1 could specifically interact with its recognition motif in a nucleosomal context (Last et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Qu et al., 2021.

claim: LEF1 was identified as a regulatory high mobility group box protein that could bind to nucleosomes.
source: For instance, HNF4A was annotated as a potential PTF active in chromatin remodeling in the liver (Qu et al., 2021), LEF1 was identified as a regulatory high mobility group box protein that could bind to nucleosomes (Steger and Workman, 1997), and CUX1 could specifically interact with its recognition motif in a nucleosomal context (Last et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Steger and Workman, 1997.

claim: CUX1 could specifically interact with its recognition motif in a nucleosomal context.
source: For instance, HNF4A was annotated as a potential PTF active in chromatin remodeling in the liver (Qu et al., 2021), LEF1 was identified as a regulatory high mobility group box protein that could bind to nucleosomes (Steger and Workman, 1997), and CUX1 could specifically interact with its recognition motif in a nucleosomal context (Last et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Last et al., 1999.

claim: 87% of all 225 TFs had negative PCC between binding motif profiles and nucleosome occupancy values.
source: Our results showed that 87% of all 225 TFs had negative PCC between binding motif profiles and nucleosome occupancy values (Figure 3b) which is consistent with the fact that nucleosomes generally restrict the access of TFs to their binding sites on DNA molecules.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 3b.

claim: 37 TFs had a statistically significant positive correlation coefficients between binding motif profile and nucleosome occupancy and could be classified as potential nucleosome binders and PTFs.
source: We have also identified 37 TFs that had a statistically significant positive correlation coefficients between binding motif profile and nucleosome occupancy and could be classified as potential nucleosome binders and PTFs (Supplementary file 1—table 9 and Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Among 37 TFs with positive correlation, there were six known PTFs: POU5F1 (OCT4), GATA3, CEBPB, ATF2, NFYA, and NFYB.
source: Among these predictions there were six known PTFs, such as POU5F1 (OCT4), GATA3, CEBPB, ATF2, NFYA, and NFYB (Supplementary file 1—table 9).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis and established knowledge about these TFs.

claim: NFYB, NFYA, and POU5F1 had low enrichment scores but were identified as nucleosome binders by correlation analysis.
source: As we mentioned previously, NFYB, NFYA, and POU5F1 had low enrichment scores, but were identified as nucleosome binders by this correlation analysis.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: NFYB, NFYA, and POU5F1 can bind to nucleosomes using certain binding arrangements but can also interact with naked DNA.
source: It could be explained by their dual nature: these factors can bind to nucleosomes using certain binding arrangements, as evident from their positive correlation coefficients, but at the same time, they can interact with the naked DNA, as evident from their low enrichment scores.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis.

claim: 16 predictions coincided with the predicted PTFs from the enrichment analysis: ATF2, BACH1, CEBPB, CTCF, ESRRA, HMBOX1, NFATC3, NFYB, SREBF2, USF1, USF2, ZNF24, ZNF274, ZNF282, ZNF460 and ZKSCAN1.
source: Supplementary file 1—table 9 shows 16 predictions that coincided with the predicted PTFs from the enrichment analysis (ATF2, BACH1, CEBPB, CTCF, ESRRA, HMBOX1, NFATC3, NFYB, SREBF2, USF1, USF2, ZNF24, ZNF274, ZNF282, ZNF460 and ZKSCAN1).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Among TFs with high PCC>0.5, there were ZKSCAN1, ESR1, NFATC3, ZBTB7B, MAX, and TBX2.
source: Among those with high PCC>0.5, there were ZKSCAN1, ESR1, NFATC3, ZBTB7B, MAX, and TBX2.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Half of TFs with high PCC>0.5 were also predicted to be pioneers by a recent study.
source: Half of them were also predicted to be pioneers by a recent study (Pop et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pop et al., 2023.

claim: CTCF was identified as having a significant correlation between binding motif profile and nucleosome occupancy for the human embryonic stem cell line (PCC = 0.1, p-value <0.05), but not for other somatic cell lines.
source: For example, CTCF was identified as having a significant correlation (although low) between binding motif profile and nucleosome occupancy for the human embryonic stem cell line (PCC = 0.1, p-value <0.05), but not for other somatic cell lines (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 3d.

claim: CTCF proteins could access the binding sites in nucleosomes and may function as PTFs in embryonic stem cells and to a lesser extent in differentiated cells.
source: Indeed, previous studies have indicated that CTCF proteins could access the binding sites in nucleosomes and may function as PTFs in embryonic stem cells and to a lesser extent in differentiated cells (Teif et al., 2012; Teif et al., 2014; Voong et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The computational analysis is able to capture the detailed features of TF binding motifs on nucleosomes.
source: This shows that our computational analysis is able to capture the detailed features of TF binding motifs on nucleosomes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation with experimental data.

claim: TFs in the first and second cluster showed that motif density increased with the distance from the dyad.
source: TFs in the first and second cluster showed that motif density increased with the distance from the dyad.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Clusters 1 and 2 include cases of canonical factors or those PTFs that preferentially interact with the ends of nucleosomal DNA from SHLs ±5 to SHL ±6.
source: These clusters include cases of canonical factors or those PTFs that preferentially interact with the ends of nucleosomal DNA from SHLs ±5 to SHL ±6.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clustering analysis.

claim: In clusters 4 and 6, TFs preferentially interact with the nucleosomal DNA around the dyad regions and SHL from ±3.5 to SHL ±5.5.
source: In clusters 4 and 6, TFs preferentially interact with the nucleosomal DNA around the dyad regions and SHL from ±3.5 to SHL ±5.5, whereas TFs from clusters 3 and 5 preferentially occupy SHL 1 to SHL ±3, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clustering analysis.

claim: TFs from clusters 3 and 5 preferentially occupy SHL 1 to SHL ±3.
source: In clusters 4 and 6, TFs preferentially interact with the nucleosomal DNA around the dyad regions and SHL from ±3.5 to SHL ±5.5, whereas TFs from clusters 3 and 5 preferentially occupy SHL 1 to SHL ±3, respectively.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clustering analysis.

claim: GATA3 factor targets nucleosomal DNA around the SHL ±5.5 position.
source: Indeed, it has been recently shown that GATA3 factor targets nucleosomal DNA around the SHL ±5.5 position (Tanaka et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tanaka et al., 2020.

claim: Many TFs from the same family and even from different cell types were assigned to the same cluster.
source: We found that many TFs from the same family and even from different cell types were assigned to the same cluster.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: All known PTFs from FOXA families belong to cluster 4.
source: For example, all known PTFs from FOXA families belong to cluster 4 and indeed it has been shown that FOXA1 can target its binding motifs to nucleosomal DNA near the dyad and linker regions (Iwafuchi-Doi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis and citation to Iwafuchi-Doi et al., 2016.

claim: FOXA1 can target its binding motifs to nucleosomal DNA near the dyad and linker regions.
source: For example, all known PTFs from FOXA families belong to cluster 4 and indeed it has been shown that FOXA1 can target its binding motifs to nucleosomal DNA near the dyad and linker regions (Iwafuchi-Doi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iwafuchi-Doi et al., 2016.

claim: There are exceptions where the same TF from different cell lines has been assigned to different clusters, such as CEBPB, CREB1, CTCF, MEF2A, NFYA, and NFYB.
source: However, there are a few exceptions, such as CEBPB, CREB1, CTCF, MEF2A, NFYA, and NFYB, where the same TF from different cell lines has been assigned to different clusters.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: TF binding to nucleosomes leads to DNA and chromatin opening and might correlate with the reprogramming potential.
source: As a result, we found that using the information on differentially open chromatin regions (open in one cell line, closed in another) leads to the highest classification accuracy in discriminating pioneer from canonical TFs. This finding supports the view that TF binding to nucleosomes leads to DNA and chromatin opening and might correlate with the reprogramming potential (Fernandez Garcia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis and citation to Fernandez Garcia et al., 2019.

claim: The classification method and data used in this study have certain limitations.
source: We should mention that our classification method and the data used in this study have certain limitations.
evidence: This is a statement acknowledging limitations of the study.

claim: Interactions of PTFs with nucleosomes may depend on binding of other factors.
source: First, interactions of PTFs with nucleosomes may depend on binding of other factors.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation based on established knowledge.

claim: PTF binding relies on specific recognition of DNA binding sites and can be governed by nucleosome dynamics.
source: Second, PTF binding relies on specific recognition of DNA binding sites and can be governed by nucleosome dynamics.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation based on established knowledge.

claim: Initial stages of binding can happen via the DNA site exposure through thermal fluctuations, leading to DNA unwrapping and the formation of DNA looping or twist defects.
source: Indeed, initial stages of binding can happen via the DNA site exposure through thermal fluctuations, leading to DNA unwrapping and the formation of DNA looping or twist defects (Poirier et al., 2009; Li et al., 2022; Brandani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: PTFs can exploit DNA unwrapping and trap nucleosomes in a partially unwrapped states.
source: PTFs can exploit DNA unwrapping and trap nucleosomes in a partially unwrapped states (Donovan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Donovan et al., 2019.

claim: The degree of spontaneous DNA unwrapping from nucleosomes depends on the incorporation of histone variants, like H2A.Z.
source: Moreover, as we showed recently, the degree of spontaneous DNA unwrapping from nucleosomes depends on the incorporation of histone variants, like H2A.Z (Li et al., 2023), which, in turn, might be needed for PTF recruitment to promote embryonic stem cell differentiation (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2023 and Li et al., 2012.

claim: Histone variant H2A.Z might be needed for PTF recruitment to promote embryonic stem cell differentiation.
source: Moreover, as we showed recently, the degree of spontaneous DNA unwrapping from nucleosomes depends on the incorporation of histone variants, like H2A.Z (Li et al., 2023), which, in turn, might be needed for PTF recruitment to promote embryonic stem cell differentiation (Li et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2012.

claim: Nucleosome positioning and stability is not uniform throughout the genome and depends on local nucleosomal DNA sequence, histone variant deposition, and epigenetic chromatin modifications.
source: Indeed, nucleosome positioning and stability is not uniform throughout the genome and depends on local nucleosomal DNA sequence, histone variant deposition, and epigenetic chromatin modifications.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: PTFs may exhibit multivalent binding recognizing not only DNA binding sites but also some parts of the histone core or histone tail regions.
source: Finally, PTFs may exhibit multivalent binding recognizing not only DNA binding sites but also some parts of the histone core or histone tail regions.
evidence: This is a statement about a limitation based on established knowledge.

claim: TFs regulate a large number of signaling pathways and their dysregulation contributes to a plethora of human diseases, including diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and many cancers.
source: TFs regulate a large number of signaling pathways and their dysregulation contributes to a plethora of human diseases, including diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, and many cancers.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Conventional TFs have been used for a long time as biomarkers and drug targets.
source: Conventional TFs have been used for a long time as biomarkers and drug targets, however, the targeted therapeutic potential of PTFs is lagging.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The targeted therapeutic potential of PTFs is lagging.
source: Conventional TFs have been used for a long time as biomarkers and drug targets, however, the targeted therapeutic potential of PTFs is lagging.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: Pronounced dinucleotide patterns were observed at specific nucleosomal DNA positions for all cell lines.
source: As a result, we observed pronounced dinucleotide patterns at specific nucleosomal DNA positions for all cell lines which are indicative of the high quality of the data and nucleosome mapping procedure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Pronounced dinucleotide patterns are indicative of the high quality of the data and nucleosome mapping procedure.
source: As a result, we observed pronounced dinucleotide patterns at specific nucleosomal DNA positions for all cell lines which are indicative of the high quality of the data and nucleosome mapping procedure (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data analysis.

claim: Two recent cryo-EM structures of the PTF SOX2-nucleosome complexes showed different mechanisms of binding.
source: For example, two recent cryo-EM structures of the PTF SOX2-nucleosome complexes showed different mechanisms of binding (Michael et al., 2020; Dodonova et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Michael et al., 2020 and Dodonova et al., 2020.

claim: Using the information on differentially open chromatin regions leads to the highest classification accuracy in discriminating pioneer from canonical TFs.
source: As a result, we found that using the information on differentially open chromatin regions (open in one cell line, closed in another) leads to the highest classification accuracy in discriminating pioneer from canonical TFs.
evidence: This is supported by the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The study verified known and predicted several dozens of new PTFs as nucleosome binders.
source: Our study has also verified the known and predicted several dozens of new PTFs as nucleosome binders (Supplementary file 1—tables 2, 4, and 9).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the data analysis.

claim: Six distinctive clusters of TF binding profiles with the nucleosomal DNA were identified.
source: Finally, we have identified six distinctive clusters of TF binding profiles with the nucleosomal DNA.
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: TFs belonging to the same cluster may exhibit potential competitive binding.
source: These clusters point to the diversity of binding motifs where TFs belonging to the same cluster may exhibit potential competitive binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clustering analysis.
